content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the client dropout condition in federated learning and focuses on how to mitigate this by leveraging the uploaded gradients from the non-dropout (active) clients for the dropout (inactive) clients. Its approach identifies the so-called "friends" (clients with similar data distributions) on-the-fly. The paper also presents a convergence analysis based on some assumptions on the presence and similarity among the clients. In particular, it proposes a method FL-FDMS that can achieve the optimal (i.e., assuming full participation) asymptotic convergence. A pratical implementation to reduce computational complexity and experimental results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 are provided to showcase the effectiveness of the method in terms of performance and friendship discovery.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- The problem is relatively well-motivated that client dropout is considered from the passive perspective instead of the proactive perspective due to practical constraints of the devices.
- The approach has theoretical guarantees.
- A principled practical technique is introduced to specifically reduce complexity while retaining the theoretical guarantee.


### Weaknesses
- Its position with existing cluster FL works can be made clearer. The related work section primarily discuss dropout and straggler-related works, very little about clutering in FL is mentioned. However, in sections 4 and 5, the knowledge about clustering is assumed: (in the paragraph after equation 13) 
    > For example, consider that clients are grouped into clusters and clients from the same cluster have the identical data distribution.Borrowing the idea of Shi et al. (2022) ... 

    The setting described by this sentence requires motivation. 

    Based on this described setting, the friendship (discovery) section bears high resemblance to the setting of clustering FL works, which inspires the following question: (1) what are the differences (2) what makes existing clustering discovery methods (some are listed below) in FL _not_ applicable here; and (3) what prevents the experimental comparison against clustering discovery methods in FL from being performed?

- The justification and/or verification of some assumptions can be strengthened.

    - In Assumption 3, $\Vert \nabla F^k (x) - \nabla f(x) \Vert^2 \leq \sigma_G^2, \forall x, \forall k \in \mathcal{K}$. This implicitly restricts the local distribution of each dataset to be somewhat close to the global distribution (over all clients) in the variance of gradient sense, it is verifiable, even if the clients can dropout arbitrarily?

    - In the paragraph below equation 8
    > Thus, by using constant learning rates $\eta$ and $\eta_L$ and assuming that $\Vert e_t \Vert^2$ is bounded ...

        Can this assumption hold? Is there some way to verify it?
    - In Assumption 4, this is required to hold $\forall w$. However, for complex models such as deep neural networks which can have highly irregular function surfaces for even slightly different objective functions (due to the difference in the local datasets), will $\sigma_{i,j}^2$ be so large that the following analysis dependent on $\sigma_{i,j}$ becomes very loose?

    - In the paragraph below equation 11
    > Nevertheless, with a decreasing and vanishing dropout rate $\alpha$, ... 

        While the following implication makes sense theoretically, but this assumption/condition of a decreasing and vanishing dropout rate seems at odds with the primary motivation of the work which is that the dropout is not controllable at all. So the justification of this condition is not so clear.

    - In Equation 14, the paper directly adopts the normalized cosine similarity for its mathematical convenience. However, this design choice may need further justification since similar works in FL already use the non-normalised cosine similarity on gradients between clients.

- The experiments can be improved in terms of selection of comparison baselines and the scale of experiments.

    - The clustered setting is only explained in the appendix. In the main text, without context or an intuition, it is difficult to see why it makes sense as a setting.
    - Following first weakness and the fact that a clustered setting is used for experiments, it is unclear why clustering FL methods are not compared here (including both the accuracy and against the friendship discovery method).
    - The baselines are not clearly explained in the main text to help the reader understand why they are included.
    - More experiments on real-world datasets would help make the method more convincing.


#### References
**Clustering FL algorithms**

Long, G., Xie, M., Shen, T., Zhou, T., Wang, X., & Jiang, J. (2022). Multi-center federated learning: clients clustering for better personalization. WWW 2022.

Ruan, Y., & Joe-Wong, C. (2022). FedSoft: Soft Clustered Federated Learning with Proximal Local Updating. AAAI 2022.


Xueyang Tang, Song Guo, Jingcai Guo. Personalized Federated Learning with Contextualized Generalization. IJCAI 2022.


**Cosine similarity of gradients in FL algorithms**

Xiaoyu Cao, Minghong Fang, Jia Liu, Neil Zhenqiang Gong. FLTrust: Byzantine-robust Federated Learning via Trust Bootstrapping. NDSS 2021.

Xinyi Xu, Lingjuan Lyu, Xingjun Ma, Chenglin Miao, Chuan Sheng Foo, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low. Gradient Driven Rewards to Guarantee Fairness in Collaborative Machine Learning. NeurIPS 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
The paper in general is clearly written, I was able to follow the main idea and most of the technical results. Some clarification questions:
- What does the constant $c$ depend on in Theorem 1?
- Why is equation 8 different from equation 44?
- Following equation 8, how does $\Psi$ change with $T$, assuming $||e_t||^2$ is upper bounded? It does not seem $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ or a constant as claimed, but rather the summation $\sum_{t=0}^{-1}$ makes it increasing in $T$.
- How is $\sigma_F^2$ determined or verified such that (after equation 12): 
> since typically $\sigma_F^2 \ll \sigma_{P}^2$  

- How is the number of friends $B_k$ determined in practice? because the threshold $\Theta_t$ depends on it.

### Quality
The paper is generally well written.

### Novelty
I think the approach has some novelty, however, I also believe some ideas used here are already present (or at least in a similar form) in existing FL literature. For instance, Theorem 1 relies on Lemma 4 of Reddi et al. (2020). The use of cosine similarity to compare/evaluate gradients is also not completely new (see references above). The friendship (discovery) section seems to bear similarity to the clustering methods in FL. 


### Reproducibility
Reproducibility is good in the sense that sufficient details are available in the appendix about the experiment and code is also provided, though I did not run the code.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mQor
content.comment:
We appreciate reviewer mQor's feedback, and we will answer these questions below.

**Weaknesses-1**. 

- Similarity-based optimization is a general idea and is not unique to clustered FL. Our method has a very different motivation and objective from existing works. In addition, we only require pair-wise similarity, which can be computed easily on the server, whereas clustered FL needs to identify a set of clients belonging to the same cluster, which incurs much higher computation and communication overhead.

-  (The knowledge about clustering is assumed): The knowledge about clustering is only assumed in one specific experiment to provide a controlled environment in order to better illustrate the performance of our friend discovery mechanism. It is not assumed in our model, algorithm or analysis. We also conducted experiments on general data distributions without the clustered structure. 


**Weaknesses-2**. 

- (Assumption 3): The global objection function $f(x)$ and hence its gradient $\nabla f(x)$ does not depend on client dropout. Thus, assumption 3 always holds by choosing a proper value of $\sigma^2_G$. 


- (Below equation 8): Under assumption 4, $\left \|| e_t \right \||^2$ can be bounded (see Appendix A.4). 


- (Assumption 4): The reviewer is correct that $\sigma^2_{i,j}$ can large due to the highly irregular function surfaces. In this case, our analysis essentially becomes a worst-case analysis but is still correct. 


- (Below equation 11): We use decreasing and vanishing dropout rate as an example to illustrate when the algorithm can converge to a stationary point in theory. In practice, for example, consider that client dropout is due to bad wireless channel conditions. When the wireless channel conditions improve over time, the client dropout rate decreases and may vanish over time. Client dropout is still not controllable but becomes less frequent. 


- (In Equation 14): Our method can use either normalized cosine similarity or non-normalized cosine similarity. The reason why we chose normalized cosine similarity is mainly because of its mathematical convenience due to its bounded value range in [0, 1]. 

**Weaknesses-3**. 

- (The clustered setting): We moved the description of the clustered setting to the appendix due to space limitation. We will move it back to the main text in the revision. 

- (The clustering FL methods): Due to the huge differences in the motivation and objective of our method and clustering FL, we did not compare with clustering FL. Again, our method does not need to identify "clusters" of clients; we only need pair-wise similarity between clients. The experiment on the clustered setting is used to provide a controlled environment to better illustrate the performance of our friend discovery mechanism. We also have experimental results on the general distribution where applying clustering FL does not make much sense but incurs unnecessary overhead. 

-  (The baselines): We moved the description of the baselines to the appendix due to space limitation. We will move it back to the main text in the revision. 

- (More experiments): The MNIST and Cifar10 are the standard datasets that are widely used in SOTA federated learning works [1-3]. However, to address the reviewer's comment, we add additional experiments on the FMNIST datasets, which are shown in the rebuttal version.

**Clarity**. 

- (Constant $c$): The constant $c$ satisfies $(\frac{1}{2} - 30\eta^2_L E^2 L^2) > c > 0$.

- (Equation 8): Thanks to the reviewer for pointing this out, we missed some parts in Eq.(8) now (5). The correct Eq.(8) is $\Psi(e_0, ..., e_{T-1}) = \frac{1 + 3\eta \eta_L LE}{c E^2 T} \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}_t[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2]$, which is same as Eq.(44) now (39).

- ($\Phi$ change with $T$): With the correct equation 8 and Assumption 4, the round-$t$ substitution error can then be bounded as $\mathbb{E}[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2] \leq \alpha^2 \sigma^2_P$, which is a constant. Furthermore, we can obtain that the upper bound in Eq.(10) is independent of time $T$.

- ($\sigma^2_F$ determined): - Friendship is defined in a general and flexible way using a parameter $\sigma^2_F$. One can always choose a large enough $\sigma^2_F$ so that friend pairs exist. Of course, with a larger $\sigma^2_F$, the theoretical performance gain using friend model substitution will be smaller but the result still holds. 

-  ($B_k$ determined): $B_{\max}$ (which is what is really needed than $B_k$) is only used in our theoretical analysis. Running our algorithm in practice only needs a rough estimate of $B_{max}$. In fact, one can simply choose $B_{max} = 1$. 

**Reference**

[1] X. G, et al. Fast federated learning in the presence of arbitrary device unavailability. NeurIPS, 2021.

[2] H. Y, et al. Achieving linear speedup with partial worker participation in non-iid federated learning. ICLR, 2021.

[3] Y. C, et al. Towards Understanding Biased Client Selection in Federated Learning. AISTATS, 2022.

content.title: Post rebuttal
content.comment:
I thank the authors for the response. Some of my questions have been addressed. Please see some of the follow-up questions.

- Regarding Assumption 3:

    > Thus, assumption 3 always holds by choosing a proper value of $\sigma_G^2$. 

    If it always holds, is it still an assumption? On the other handing, increasing the value of $\sigma_G^2$ to ensure the assumption holds, will it make the result less useful?

- Regarding $\sigma_{i,j}$:
    > In this case, our analysis essentially becomes a worst-case analysis but is still correct.

    Could the authors comment on how useful the worst-case analysis would be? Is it possible that the correct analysis cannot provide insight because it is too loose? 

- Regarding vanishing dropout rate:

    > When the wireless channel conditions improve over time, the client dropout rate decreases and may vanish over time. 

    While this makes sense theoretically, its applicability can be strengthened. Specifically, why is it that the wireless channel conditions improve over time instead of deteriorate? The argument for the vanishing dropout rate can bade made more convincing. 

- Regarding cosine similarity:

    > Our method can use either normalized cosine similarity or non-normalized cosine similarity. 

    Does it mean the algorithm can use both cosine similarities or the analysis can use both? What has to change if the non-normalized cosine similarity is used?

- Regarding clustered setting:

    > Due to the huge differences in the motivation and objective of our method and clustering FL, we did not compare with clustering FL. 

    If there are "huge differences" in the motivation and objective of the proposed method and clustered FL, why is it a suitable experimental setting? 

- Regarding $\sigma_F^2$ and $B_\max$:
    
    > One can always choose a large enough $\sigma_F^2$ so that friend pairs exist.

    > In fact, one can simply choose $B_\max= 1$.

    Is it that increasing $\sigma_F^2$ will increase $B_k$ in general which then increases $B_\max= 1$? If so, what is the rationale for the user to increase $\sigma_F^2$ while keeping $B_\max$ to be small (i.e., $1$)?

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies federated learning (FL) where clients may dropout in an uncontrolled manner. A convergence analysis has been made to include the error caused by dropout, where the effect of dropout has been modeled as a substitute update. Then, a method called FL with Friend Discovery and Model Substitution (FL-FDMS) has been proposed, which substitutes dropout clients' updates with other active clients' updates that are similar to the dropout clients. Empirical results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets have shown that FL-FDMS improves the performance compared to some baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem of client dropout in FL is important and has practical relevance.
- The idea of using substitute updates in the analysis of FL with client dropout is interesting.

Weaknesses:
- The practical value of the proposed FL-FDMS algorithm is limited. The computation of pairwise similarity would not work with secure aggregation. For a large-scale cross-device FL system, it is also likely that some devices may only participate once or in a few rounds throughout the entire training process. In this case it is unlikely to be possible to compute the pairwise similarity among all the clients. 
- The theoretical analysis follows mostly standard steps, hence the novelty is somewhat limited. The idea of identifying similar clients is also similar to clustering, such as [a]. Overall, the idea of FL-FDMS is relatively straightforward. 
- Some results are questionable or otherwise not fully explained. For example, it is unclear how the first inequality in Eq. (10) is obtained; the definition of $\Psi$ in Eq. (8) is different from that in Eqs. (67)-(68) in the appendix (in the supplementary material), so it must be wrong at one of these two places. It is also counterintuitive that $\bar{\Psi}$ decreases in $E$ in Eqs. (10)-(11); more explanation is needed on why this is the case.

[a] Fraboni et al. Clustered Sampling: Low-Variance and Improved Representativity for Clients Selection in Federated Learning. ICML 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The motivation of this work is clear, but some parts are unclear when it comes to technical details (see weaknesses above). In addition, there are some minor issues:
- $E$ is defined as the number of 'epochs' in the paper but is used as the number of SGD iterations in the analysis. Please change 'epochs' to 'iterations'. The notion of one epoch means one full pass through the entire dataset, which includes multiple SGD iterations.
- Eq. (9) is the gap in local updates (a.k.a. pseudo gradients) that includes multiple steps of SGD updates. It would be better to use a different letter (instead of $\sigma$) here, to differentiate from the variance in gradients defined earlier.
- Above Eq. (11), it mentions "decaying learning rate". Note that the learning rate here is not really decaying, since it does not change in $t$ and only depends on $T$. The "decaying learning rate" is usually used to refer to the case of decaying in $t$, so to avoid confusion it should not be used here.
- Below Eq. (11), it mentions "decreasing and vanishing dropout rate $\alpha$. It is not clear why the dropout rate may ever vanish in practice.
- The colors in the figures are a bit hard to distinguish clearly. 
- There are some typos in the paper. For example, on page 5, SDG -> SGD.

Quality: The quality can be improved.

Novelty: The novelty is somewhat limited, as explained under weaknesses above.

Reproducibility: The code has been included, which is good. I didn't try to run it though. Overall, the proposed method seems easy to implement, but it would be nice if the appendix can include the pseudocode of the full FL-FDMS algorithm.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an interesting problem, but has drawbacks in terms of practicality and theoretical analysis. The novelty is a bit limited but probably OK.

content.title: Response to Reviewer tupj
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer tupj for the thoughtful suggestions, and we will answer these questions below.

**Weaknesses-1**. 
- For the secure aggregation problem, we face the same challenges as other previous works [1] [2] that need to determine the client relationships or client clustering. To prevent information leakage, we can create dummy or encrypted ids for clients. For example, in work [3] the authors propose generating a unique ID to hide the user's original ids to prevent information leakage, while in work [4], an extended Fo-SDD scheme protects the ids of the clients .

- Our proposed algorithm works well under certain reasonable assumptions. In particular, assumption 6 indirectly parameterizes the longest time for which a client can be inactive via the parameter $\beta$. Our convergence bound is general, which works for any value of $\beta \in (0, 1]$. Similar assumptions were also made in existing FL works, e.g., [5], which require that the dropout client cannot be inactive for a long time.

**Weaknesses-2**. 
- The convergence analysis partly follows previous work but we offer a more general convergence analysis where clients can submit substitute (inaccurate) local model updates. Our result shows how convergence depends on accumulative substitution errors. This is new knowledge in the FL literature since most FL works only consider the unbiased partial client participation problem. In sum, we believe our paper is novel and its technical contribution is considerable. 

- Our method relies on identifying pair-wise similar clients to run model substitutions. Computing client similarities also appears in clustering in FL but this alone does not weaken our novelty because similarity is a general idea that has been exploited in many other problems beyond FL. Our method has a very different motivation and objective from existing works. In addition, we only require pair-wise similarity, which can be computed easily on the server, while clustered FL needs to identify a set of clients belonging to the same cluster, which incurs much higher computation and communication overhead. 

**Weaknesses-3**. 
- Thanks to the reviewer for pointing this out, we missed some parts in Eq.(8)  (now Eq.(5)). The correct Eq.(8) is $\Psi(e_0, ..., e_{T-1}) = \frac{1 + 3\eta \eta_L LE}{c E^2 T} \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}_t[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2]$, which is same as Eq.(44) (now Eq.(39)). With Assumption 4, the round-$t$ substitution error can then be bounded as $\mathbb{E}[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2] \leq \alpha^2 \sigma^2_P$, which is a constant. Furthermore, we can obtain that the upper bound in Eq.(10) (now Eq.(7)) is independent of time $T$.

-  $\bar{\Psi}$ does not decrease in $E$. This is because $\sigma^2_P$ is used to bound the local model update difference, which also depends on $E$. Increasing $E$ in fact also increases $\sigma^2_P$ and hence $\bar{\Psi}$ does not decrease with $E$.


**Clarity**. 

- Thanks. Those have been fixed in our rebuttal version.

- We use decreasing and vanishing dropout rate as an example to illustrate when the algorithm can converge to a stationary point in theory. In practice, for example, consider that client dropout is due to bad wireless channel conditions. When the wireless channel conditions improve over time, the client dropout rate decreases and may vanish over time. 



**Reference**

[1] Y Ruan, et al. Fedsoft: Soft clustered federated learning with proximal local updating. AAAI, Vol. 36. No. 7. 2022.

[2] G, Avishek, et al. An efficient framework for clustered federated learning. NeurIPS, :19586-19597, 2020.

[3] Z, Samman, et al. "Fog computing over IoT: A secure deployment and formal verification." IEEE Access 5 (2017): 27132-27144.

[4] N, Jianbing, et al. Providing task allocation and secure deduplication for mobile crowdsensing via fog computing. TDSC  (2018): 581-594.

[5] X. Gu, et al. Fast federated learning in the presence of arbitrary device unavailability. NeurIPS, :12052–12064, 2021.

content.title: Reply to Authors
content.comment:
Thanks for the response. I feel that some concerns are not fully addressed, especially the ones mentioned by Reviewer mQor below.  For this reason, I keep my score the same. Some detailed comments on the authors' response to my review are as follows.

> For example, in work [3] the authors propose generating a unique ID to hide the user's original ids to prevent information leakage, while in work [4], an extended Fo-SDD scheme protects the ids of the clients.

I'm not sure whether this completely solves the problem. If the IDs are completely random, then the server would not know which pair of clients the similarity is being computed for. So there needs to be a unique ID for each client. Having a unique client ID makes it possible for the server to track the updates from each client. When there are multiple updates from the same client, it would be easier for the server to invert the model to infer the input data.

> we offer a more general convergence analysis where clients can submit substitute (inaccurate) local model updates

In all analyses of SGD algorithms, the local updates are "inaccurate" due to the presence of SGD noise.

> most FL works only consider the unbiased partial client participation problem

Biased participation has been considered in recent work such as:
- Fast Federated Learning in the Presence of Arbitrary Device Unavailability, NeurIPS 2021.
- Anarchic Federated Learning, ICML 2022.

In some sense, the compensation using friends' models seems to be somewhat similar to the compensation using historical gradients in these papers.

> When the wireless channel conditions improve over time, the client dropout rate decreases and may vanish over time.

This is not a valid practical scenario as also pointed out by Reviewer mQor.

-----------------------------

Overall, I feel that the paper has the potential to become a good piece of work, but several technical details need to be carefully thought through and fixed accordingly. In particular, the authors are encouraged to clearly identify the key contributions and limitations in the result. It is OK to have limitations, but they should be clearly stated in the paper instead of trying to "hide" them.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AVQE
content.comment:
We thank reviewer AVQE for the feedback and respond to each concern below.

**Concerns-a**. 

- First of all, if a client is always inactive, we can consider that the inactive client does not exist because it never participates in the training. Secondly, assumption 6 indirectly parameterizes the longest time for which a client can be inactive via the parameter $\beta$. Our convergence bound is general, which works for any value of $\beta \in (0, 1]$. Thirdly, there are similar assumptions made in existing FL works [1], which require that the dropout client cannot be inactive for a long time.

**Concerns-b**. 
- We mentioned in the paragraph under assumption 5 that this assumption could be relaxed so that friends may not be present in every round when a client drops out, and we covered the relaxed case in Appendix B.

- Friendship is defined in a general and flexible way using a parameter $\sigma^2_F$. One can always choose a large enough $\sigma^2_F$ so that friend pairs exist. Of course, with a larger $\sigma^2_F$, the theoretical performance gain using friend model substitution will be smaller but the result still holds. We also show our FDMS algorithm under a more general non-iid case in the experiment, and the result is still better than doing nothing at all or using staled models. 

**Concerns-c**. 
- The averaged similarity score is calculated based on the uploaded model and does not require any additional information from the client except maybe the ids of the clients. To prevent information leakage, we can create dummy or encrypted ids for clients.  For example, in work [2] the authors propose generating a unique ID to hide the user's original ids to prevent information leakage, while in work [3], an extended Fo-SDD scheme protects the ids of the clients.


**Reference**

[1] X. Gu, et al. Fast federated learning in the presence of arbitrary device unavailability. NeurIPS, 12052–12064, 2021.

[2] Z, Samman, et al. Fog computing over IoT: A secure deployment and formal verification. IEEE Access 5 (2017): 27132-27144.

[3] N, Jianbing, et al. Providing task allocation and secure deduplication for mobile crowdsensing via fog computing. TDSC  (2018): 581-594.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considered the problem of client dropouts and the resultant partial client participation in federated learning (FL), for which the server has no control. The authors reformulated the problem as an equivalent case in FL where the missing clients are treated by substitute local updates. The authors designed a friend discovery mechanism to mitigate the impact of dropouts. The authors also carried out experiments to verify their theoretical claims.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The problem of dropouts in FL is an important problem in FL.

2. The paper is well-written and clearly presented.

Weaknesses:

1. The proposed friend substitution mechanism, though interesting, could be hard to implement in real-world FL systems with a large number of devices. On the other hand, for FL systems with a small number of devices, a friend/substitute may be hard to find.

2. The convergence analysis techniques in this paper largely follow the standard federated averaging framework in the literature (e.g., references [2-3]). Hence, the theoretical contributions are limited.

3. The authors argued that the constant $\bar{\Psi}$ in Eq. (10) is independent of time $T$. However, this independence is not clear since it's a summation that depends on $T$ (see Eq.(8)). The authors need to elaborate more on this since this claim is an important result for the rest of the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7guq
content.comment:
We thank reviewer 7guq for the feedback and respond to each concern below.

**Weaknesses-1**. 

- Cross-device FL with extremely many devices and cross-silo FL where the clients are large organizations are only part of the FL application scenarios. There are many other FL scenarios where the number of devices is moderately large. For example, consider FL for industrial IoT monitoring [1, 2] and agricultural sensing [3]. In these applications, the number of devices is typically tens to hundreds and the proposed friend model substitution mechanism can be easily employed to address the client dropout problem.

- Even if the number of devices is very large, our mechanism can be adapted to reduce the complexity. In the paper, we already proposed one non-friend client elimination approach. Another approach is to sample only a subset of non-dropout clients and compute their similarity scores instead of using all non-dropout clients in every round. 

**Weaknesses-2**. 

- The convergence analysis partly follows [4] but we offer a more general convergence analysis where clients can submit substitute (inaccurate) local model updates. Our result shows how convergence depends on accumulative substitution errors. This is new knowledge in the FL literature since most FL works only consider the unbiased partial client participation problem. In sum, we believe our paper is novel and its technical contribution is considerable. 

**Weaknesses-3**. 
- Thanks to the reviewer for pointing this out, we missed some parts in Eq.(8) (now Eq.(5)). The correct Eq.(8) is $\Psi(e_0, ..., e_{T-1}) = \frac{1 + 3\eta \eta_L LE}{c E^2 T} \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}_t[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2]$, which is same as Eq.(44) (now Eq.(39)). With Assumption 4, the round-$t$ substitution error can then be bounded as $\mathbb{E}[\left \|| e_t \right \||^2] \leq \alpha^2 \sigma^2_P$, which is a constant. Furthermore, we can obtain that the upper bound in Eq.(10) (now Eq.(7)) is independent of time $T$.

**Reference**

[1] Y. Liu, et al. Deep anomaly detection for time-series data in industrial IoT: A communication-efficient on-device federated learning approach. IEEE IoT Journal, 8(8):6348-6358, 2020.

[2] W. Sun, et al. Adaptive federated learning and digital twin for industrial internet of things. IEEE Trans. Industrial Informatics,17(8):5605–5614, 2020.

[3] P.t Kumar, et al. Pefl: Deep privacy-encoding-based federated learning framework for smart agriculture. IEEE Micro, 42(1):33–40, 2021.

[4] H. Yang, M. Fang, and J. Liu. Achieving linear speedup with partial worker participation in non-iid federated learning. ICLR, 2021.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper studies the important question of client dropout, i.e. partial client participation in federated learning, for which the server has no control. 

The provided theoretical convergence guarantees were appreciated, but deemed a bit incremental in terms of techniques used. On the empirical results, reviewers also commented on some limitations (such as the required computation of the partial similarity matrix). Positioning in the already established set of many related works can be improved as well.
Unfortunately consensus among the reviewers remained that the paper in its current form remains narrowly below the bar even after the discussion phase.

We hope the detailed feedback helps to strengthen the paper for a future occasion.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Concerns on level of novelty (theory and practice). Though it can be argued it might reach the bar narrowly
